subsection: 5. The Civil War, state building and the consolidation of democracy, 1922–1932

notes.h: The split and the outbreak of the Civil War, 1922
notes.b: Ratification of the Treaty split the IRA and the Dáil. Anti-Treaty forces occupied Dublin buildings in the spring of 1922, and the Free State attacked them in June.
points: After ratification, the anti-Treaty IRA occupied the Four Courts in Dublin in April 1922, and the Provisional Government, with Collins at its head, was caught between its own army and its political commitments.
The Free State's attack on the Four Courts on 28 June 1922 marked the start of the Civil War; the building was shelled and its occupiers forced to surrender.
Field Marshal Sir Henry Wilson, a unionist MP, was assassinated in London on 22 June 1922 by two IRA men, an act that heightened British pressure on the Free State.
Arthur Griffith died of a stroke on 12 August 1922, and Michael Collins was killed in an ambush at Béal na Bláth, Co. Cork, on 22 August 1922.
After Collins's death, William Cosgrave succeeded him as chairman of the Provisional Government.
The anti-Treaty forces were led by Liam Lynch, who was killed in April 1923, and by de Valera's political wing, which opposed the Free State but was not in control of the fighting.

notes.h: The course of the Civil War, 1922–1923
notes.b: The Civil War was fought mainly in the south and west, with the Free State army gaining the upper hand through its control of towns and its heavier equipment.
points: The Free State army, made up largely of former British army and IRA veterans of the pro-Treaty side, used artillery and armoured cars against the anti-Treaty IRA in Dublin and along the western roads.
The anti-Treaty IRA relied on guerrilla tactics, raids and ambushes, and it was short of arms, funds and organisation.
Childers was executed on 24 November 1922 after being convicted by a Free State military court of possessing a small pistol, a gift from Collins.
Four anti-Treaty leaders, Rory O'Connor, Liam Mellows, Joe McKelvey and Richard Barrett, were executed in December 1922 in reprisal for the killing of a Free State TD.
The Free State used emergency powers and military courts; about seventy-seven men were executed during the war, according to commonly cited figures (the exact number is contested).
On 24 May 1923 the anti-Treaty leadership, with de Valera's backing, ordered a ceasefire and the dumping of arms, which ended the fighting.
The Civil War left deep divisions and bitterness, and many republicans refused to take their seats in the Dáil for years afterwards.

notes.b: The Cumann na nGaedheal government built the institutions of the Free State: a constitution, a police force, a civil service and courts, and it sought to end the Civil War's divisions by firm action.
points: The Constitution of the Irish Free State, adopted in December 1922, provided for a parliament, a government responsible to the Dáil, and a Governor-General.
The Garda Síochána was established in 1922 as an unarmed civil police force, distinct from the Army and drawing on the Civic Guard.
The civil service, the courts and the local government system were kept largely as they had been under British rule, which gave the new state continuity.
The Army Mutiny of March 1924, when officers at the Curragh objected to demobilisation orders, was defused by the government's firm response, and several officers resigned.
The Boundary Commission crisis of 1924–25 threatened the Free State's territory; the Tripartite Agreement of 3 December 1925 confirmed the existing border, and the Free State accepted it.
The Public Safety Acts gave the government emergency powers to deal with armed opposition, and Kevin O'Higgins, the Minister for Justice, was the main champion of this legislation.
The Shannon Scheme was approved in 1925, the Electricity Supply Board was set up in 1927, and the Ardnacrusha power station on the Shannon opened in 1929.

notes.b: The government's challenge came from de Valera's Fianna Fáil, which decided to enter the Dáil in 1927 and won power in 1932, the first peaceful transfer of power in the state's history.
points: Fianna Fáil was founded in May 1926 by de Valera and others who had left Sinn Féin, and it argued that the Dáil oath could be taken as an empty formula.
The Electoral Amendment Act of 1927 required candidates to take the oath, and Fianna Fáil TDs took their seats in August 1927 after they signed the oath.
Kevin O'Higgins was assassinated by anti-Treaty republicans in July 1927, a sign of the continuing threat to the state.
The Cumann na nGaedheal government lost support through its economic policies, including cuts in public spending, and was defeated in the 1932 general election.
Fianna Fáil won 72 seats in the February 1932 general election; with Labour's support, de Valera formed a government in March 1932, and the Cosgrave government handed over power peacefully.

notes.b: Cosgrave led the pro-Treaty government from Collins's death in 1922 until 1932. He is judged as a cautious and effective administrator who secured the state but who was defeated by a more radical opposition.
points: William Thomas Cosgrave (1880–1965) was a Sinn Féin member, Dublin councillor and TD who took the pro-Treaty side in 1921–22.
He became chairman of the Provisional Government after Collins's death in August 1922, and then President of the Executive Council of the Free State in December 1922.
He led Cumann na nGaedheal from its founding in 1923, and his government stressed legality, the rule of law and fiscal conservatism.
He presided over the Army Mutiny, the Boundary Commission crisis and the Shannon scheme, and defended the Free State against both armed republicans and criticism of the Treaty.
Contemporaries admired his firmness and his refusal to bargain with the armed republicans; his critics saw him as cautious and too close to the business and farming interests.

Historians tend to credit his government with the survival of parliamentary democracy and the peaceful handover of 1932, while noting its economic conservatism and its reluctance to challenge the Catholic and conservative character of the state.

notes.h: Assessment: the Cosgrave governments' achievements and limits
notes.b: Judgements of the period depend on whether success is measured by the survival of the state and its institutions or by its response to economic and social problems.
points: Achievement: the Free State survived the Civil War, the Army Mutiny and the assassination of O'Higgins, and it built a working parliamentary system.
Achievement: the peaceful transfer of power in 1932 showed that the state's democratic institutions could survive a change of government.
Limit: the government's economic policies, including cuts and reliance on free trade, failed to protect the poor from the Depression and left the state dependent on British markets.
Limit: the government's use of emergency powers and military courts during the Civil War was criticised by republicans and by later historians as a harsh response.
Contemporary view: the government's supporters saw it as the defender of legality; its opponents saw it as the government of a narrow elite.
Later view: historians disagree about whether the Cosgrave governments laid the foundations for the state's later success or whether they entrenched conservative and sectarian attitudes.

keyTerms.definition: The government set up in January 1922 under Collins to prepare for the Free State, which Cosgrave led from August 1922.
The conflict between pro-Treaty Free State forces and anti-Treaty IRA forces from June 1922 to May 1923.
The Irish Free State, the dominion established in 1922 with a Governor-General and a parliament in Dublin.
The pro-Treaty party founded in 1923, which governed the Free State until 1932.
The Free State's unarmed civil police force, established in 1922 and distinct from the Army.
The March 1924 crisis at the Curragh, when officers objected to government orders to demobilise anti-Treaty veterans.
Emergency laws of 1923 and 1927 giving the Free State government powers to deal with armed opposition, which Kevin O'Higgins championed.
The 1927 Act that required Dáil candidates to take the oath, enabling Fianna Fáil to enter the Dáil.
The republican party founded by de Valera in 1926 that entered the Dáil in 1927 and won power in 1932.
The hydroelectric project on the River Shannon at Ardnacrusha, opened in 1929, which was the first major state electricity project.
